articles.title: The Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” is deceiving
articles.content: Holy freaking cow. I saw the new Elizabeth Holmes documentary, You Can See Everything , last night, and I genuinely can’t type fast enough to express how mind-bending it was. I’ve seen a lot of chatter online about whether Elizabeth Holmes is a liar, whether she deserves to be in prison for her failed startup Theranos, and whether the documentary is too sympathetic to her. But that’s not even remotely close to what I took away from it. As we walked out, my husband asked me, “So what did you think?” And I just responded with, “Forget Elizabeth Holmes. That was a masterpiece in storytelling.” I walked in expecting that the filmmakers were going to tell us a story about deception. What I did not expect is that they were deceiving us — the viewers — in real time. An entire theater full of grown adults was falling for it. At one point, people were shouting so loudly at the screen that I couldn’t hear the dialogue. I heard a woman yell, “Criminal!” — and it wasn’t directed at Elizabeth Holmes. I’ve never experienced anything like that in a movie theater. It was emotion, and it was visceral. What makes the documentary so brilliant is that it forces you to confront how much of what you believe about another person comes how their story has been told to you. And we are so so susceptible to this that it’s scary. Think about Elizabeth Holmes. How much of your opinion of her comes from the facts of her criminal case & how much comes from the images and/or videos and/or TV dramas you’ve seen over the years? I remember one Halloween when the Theranos scandal was at its peak, it seemed like everyone was dressed in a black turtleneck carrying tiny vials of fake blood. Holmes was everywhere. But the thing that often gets lost in the retelling of her story is that Holmes was actually acquitted of all four charges related to defrauding patients. She’s in prison because a jury found that she knowingly misled investors who poured more than $700 million into the startup. That’s a significant distinction, but as a society, we don’t love nuance. Just tell us — is she good or is she bad? Is she a liar or is she not? I recently wrote about a fascinating experiment Canon conducted in 2015. Six photographers were asked to photograph the same man in the same location. The twist was that each photographer was given a different description of him: a millionaire, a convict, a fisherman, an alcoholic, a psychic, and a lifesaver. The resulting portraits were wildly different. A Canon rep said, “A photograph is shaped more by the person behind the camera than by what’s in front of it.” Now imagine that principle applied to an entire three-hour documentary. Over the course of the film, directors Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder managed to make a theater full of people with fully developed pre-frontal cortexes repeatedly reconsider what they believed about the people on screen. They did it through camera angles, close-ups, editing, and the order in which information was revealed.
articles.summary: 作者批评伊丽莎白·霍姆斯新纪录片《You Can See Everything》存在误导性叙述，引发对纪录片客观性的质疑。

articles.title: The Intel 8087 chip: floating-point addition and subtraction
articles.content: In 1980, Intel introduced the 8087, a chip that made floating-point operations much faster in the IBM PC and other systems. Although the 8087 supports advanced operations such as tangents, square roots, and logarithms, this article focuses on basic arithmetic operations: addition and subtraction. The 8087 provided a spectacular speed improvement over the 8086 processor, speeding up addition by a factor of almost 100, and complicated operations by even more. 1 In this article, I examine the 8087's microcode and circuitry to explain exactly how floating-point addition and subtraction are implemented, including numerous special cases for infinities and other special values. To explore the 8087's circuitry, I popped the lid off a chip with a chisel and used a microscope to create the high-resolution image below. The microcode ROM is the large rectangular region in the center of the die, holding the 1648 micro-instructions that control the chip. The bottom half of the chip (red box) is the datapath, the circuitry that performs floating-point calculations on 80-bit values. 2 A close-up of the 8087's datapath, showing functional blocks that are used for addition and subtraction. Click this image (or any other) for a larger version. Zooming in on the datapath shows the functional blocks that are important for addition and subtraction. The key component is the integer adder, located in the center. It receives one argument from the B register and another argument from a component such as the temporary registers or the stack registers. The adder's output is stored in the sum register. The shifter can shift the bits in a value to the left or the right. The shifter occupies a lot of space on the die because its circuitry allows a value to be rapidly shifted by an arbitrary number of bits. Floating-point operations make heavy use of the shifter to align values; the leading zero circuitry counts the number of zero bits or bytes on the left of a value so they can be shifted away. The exponent converter processes exponents, detecting overflows and underflows. These specialized circuits helped the 8087 achieve its high performance. Floating-point addition and subtraction Most computers use integers as their basic representation for numbers. But many applications need to use numbers with a fractional part, such as 1.23. Moreover, integers have a very limited range: a 32-bit integer can express numbers from about -2 billion to 2 billion. To solve these problems, 3 computers usually implement floating-point numbers, which provide fractional numbers over an enormous range. In most cases, a floating-point number is represented by sign × significand × 2 exponent . The significand is a binary number of the form 1.bbb… : a leading 1, followed by the binary point (the binary equivalent of the decimal point) and the rest of the bits. 4 In a binary number, each bit represents a power of 2. articles.title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents: LLM agents that think in latent space, act through text
articles.content: [Submitted on 13 Oct 2026] Title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents Authors: Jiaru Zou , Yunzhe Qi , Sirui Chen , Federico Bianchi , Shang Zhu , Pan Lu , Jingrui He , James Zou View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent's continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning: HybridSFT stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. We evaluate HybridAgent at 3 model scales across 11 benchmarks covering mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning. Compared with frontier LLM Agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent methods, HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while delivering 35.5%-54.7% token reduction, 1.8x-2.6x faster inference, and 2.7x-3.7x cost savings. Code and data are available at this https URL .

articles.title: Someone behind the software
articles.content: I think good products carry something of the people who make them. Their experience, what they care about, and how they think things should work. You might not know who those people are, but you can feel their perspective in the product. The industry often talks about software as though it comes out of a factory. You collect requirements, build features, and measure whether they work. Follow the process and you should get a good result. Now we're talking automating this whole pipeline with agents. But two teams can talk to similar customers, have access to the same technology, and make very different things. The difference comes from how they understand what they see and the style they go about building it. The founder background or company DNA also shapes this a lot. At Linear , we have always valued intuition over process or data. I think people sometimes understand that as making decisions based on personal preference, without much thought or evidence. What we mean by it is that your intuition develops through experience and understanding. You work on something, talk to customers, make mistakes, and learn what to pay attention to. The intuition is your point of view on something, and forcing to use your judgment, not hide behind faceless data. Before we launched, we talked to people across companies and roles about how they worked. We had our own frustrations with this type software, but those conversations helped us understand what mattered beyond our own experience. Our perspective got better after those conversations. So eventually the products develops a character through what its makers pay attention to, what they decide not to do and what they keep working on after it technically works. I sometimes think of this as the soul of a product. You feel that someone cares about how the whole thing comes together. A feature can work perfectly well on its own and still make the product worse. Recognizing that requires some belief about what the product should be. Someone has to make the call, then stay close enough to customers to see whether they were right. Recently, many products are starting to feel messy to me, including products from very successful companies. There seems to be more thought going into what the technology can do and what can be added than the form it should take. The product changes are primarily additive, not improving the core problem. I think the reasons for this is that it's lot easier to add new capabilities, than rethink existing capabilities. So each product becomes a collection of abilities, without actually having unified point of view. I wonder whether some of this comes from how the work is organized. Individuals work with agents to produce changes independently, each operating a small software factory. Each change might make sense on its own, but together they start to resemble Frankenstein’s monster rather than a carefully shaped sculpture. articles.title: Free Pascal compiler now supports dynamic packages
articles.content: Dynamic Packages I am pleased to announce the first release of full dynamic package support for the Free Pascal Compiler and the Lazarus IDE. This feature has been a long time coming for the ecosystem, but a complete implementation is now available for Dynamic packages allow users to create and install components, controls, and Lazarus extensions in seconds without rebuilding the entire IDE. They can also be used in your own programs to develop and deploy plugins that expose native Pascal classes and types through dynamic package libraries. To support this functionality, I have made numerous improvements to the compiler, its runtime, and the Lazarus IDE. I have also created additional IDE extensions to improve the experience of working with Lazarus packages. All installers include dynamic package support Dynamic packages are implemented as standard shared library files for Linux, Windows, and macOS. They contain additional metadata generated by the compiler that can be inspected and queried using new RTL units. The runtime also includes mechanisms for safely preserving thread variables and managing dynamic types, such as strings and dynamic arrays, between programs and packages or between multiple packages. Video: Dynamic Packages Example When deploying your program, you can still bundle everything into a single executable. Alternatively, you can divide it into multiple dynamic packages that can be replaced while your program is running, providing a plugin system. Restrictions Dynamic packages come with a few restrictions. First, a unit contained in a package cannot have the same name as the package itself. I have enhanced the default package system so that the generated Pascal source file automatically appends the word Package to the package name. For example, if you create a package called ElectroTools.lpk , the source file listing all the units contained in the package will be named ElectroToolsPackage.pas instead of ElectroTools.pas . Another restriction is that unit names must be unique across packages. If someone else has written a unit named Widgets, you cannot install another package containing a unit with the same name. You must either choose which package to install or rename one of the conflicting units. Dynamic packages are also larger than ordinary shared libraries because they contain a map of everything inside them. Stripping a dynamic package removes the metadata required for it to function as a dynamic package. articles.title: Dogs seem to agree with humans that 'bouba' is round and 'kiki' is spiky
articles.content: Picture a shape called 'Bouba'. What features does it have? Is it angular, rounded, soft, hard? What about a shape called 'Kiki'? There's no correct answer to this – the words are made up. But for some strange reason, most people who are asked this question – regardless of the language or alphabet they use to speak or write – agree that Kiki is spiky, and Bouba is round. This fascinating psychological experiment was first conceived in the 1920s, and it suggests there may be something universal about the way we humans connect visual information, like shapes, with sounds. Now, a new study published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences suggests even our canine companions might follow this trend. The shapes used in the 'bouba/kiki' experiments. ( Andrew Dunn/Wikimedia Commons/CC BY-SA 3.0) Animal behaviorist Eleonora Biffi at the University of Parma in Italy led the research. She and her team recruited 70 domestic dogs to participate in two almost identical experiments. The first experiment involved 51 dogs and their owners. Each dog/owner pair entered a room set up with a screen and a speaker to the left, and another screen and speaker to the right. After giving the dog an opportunity to explore the room and get settled in, the owner sat with them, facing the middle of the setup while the screens and speakers played. Over roughly 15 minutes, the screens and speakers alternated through different combinations of a human saying either 'Bouba' or 'Kiki' over the speakers, and the two shapes above swapping between the left and right screens. Meanwhile, a GoPro recorded each dog during the trials. The researchers later fed these videos into an AI designed to track where the dogs' heads were pointing, a stand-in for where they were looking, so they could check for any statistically significant patterns that might occur above random chance. The second experiment, which involved 19 other dogs, was identical in design except that the owners wore headphones playing rock music to stop them from hearing the 'Bouba' and 'Kiki' sounds. The idea here was to remove any owner cues the dogs might have been following. Setup of the experiment with the two screens, and steps of the computational analyses with dog's head detection and angular vision detection. (Biffi et al., Proc. R. Soc. B , 2026) Overall, "dogs looked significantly more at the rounded shape while 'Bouba' was played, and they looked at and explored the spiky shape when 'Kiki' was played," Biffi and team report . The main difference between the two experiments was that dogs in study 1 showed a general bias toward looking at the spiky shapes. That bias disappeared in study 2, when their owners were wearing headphones. "It could be hypothesized that the dogs were influenced by the owners' unintentional cues. articles.title: Java sealed classes and exhaustive pattern matching
articles.content: Java 17 introduced sealed classes , which allow you to explicitly list the allowed sub-types of an interface or base class. For example, here’s a toy example using a sealed interface and records (inner classes are implicitly added to the permitted sub-types if an explicit list is not given): public sealed interface SealedType { record TypeA() implements SealedType {} record TypeB() implements SealedType {} static SealedType of(String type) { return switch (type) { case “A” -> new TypeA(); case “B” -> new TypeB(); default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException(); }; } } If you are familiar with functional programming languages with algebraic datatypes, you can view this as similar to a datatype declaration in Haskell or ML: data SealedType = TypeA | TypeB We can then use this in a simple Main class: void main(String[] args) { var val = SealedType.of(args[0]); System.out.println(switch (val) { case SealedType.TypeA() -> “A”; case SealedType.TypeB() -> “B”; }); } OK, not so exciting. But one thing to note here is that we didn’t have to add a default clause to the switch expression in our main method. This is because sealed classes (and enums) enable exhaustiveness checking : the compiler knows exactly what the possible cases are, and so can check if you have covered them all. If you have, then you don’t need a default clause. If you forget one (and don’t have a default clause), then you get a compile-time error. This is great when you want to ensure that all uses of some type do cover all of the cases, but it does introduce a new type of breaking change: adding a new sub-type to a sealed class/interface may break consumers of that code. For example, adding a new TypeC case to our example will cause the main method to fail to compile due to the missing case. So if you export a sealed type in your API then adding a new subtype is a breaking change that would require a major version bump (if you’re following SemVer). Compile-time or runtime error? Although Java will produce a compile-time error for a non-exhaustive switch when you compile the consumer (main in this case), it cannot do so if the consumer is not recompiled when the sealed type changes. For example, suppose that we extend our SealedType with another case: public sealed interface SealedType { record TypeA() implements SealedType {} record TypeB() implements SealedType {} record TypeC() implements SealedType {} static SealedType of(String type) { return switch (type) { case “A” -> new TypeA(); case “B” -> new TypeB(); case “C” -> new TypeC(); default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException(); }; } } If we just recompiled SealedType.java and don’t recompile Main, then we end up with a runtime exception if we trigger the new case: Here we have the new MatchException being thrown. The Javadoc notes this potential issue with separate compilation, and also some corner-cases with nulls in patterns. So even if you were hoping that using sealed classes would statically ensure that you update all consu

articles.title: It's enough - vibecoding tag crossed from useless to harmful
articles.content:
The vibecoding tag has been getting more and more useless for a while now. It lost the original meaning as the culture of software engineering with LLMs matured a bit. It got silly when posts talking about LLMs in general got tagged. It got useless when posts even mentioning some project created with LLMs in passing got tagged. Now it actually got harmful to the community when tagging posts turns away very valuable members https://lobste.rs/c/vecuxj

I sighed and moved on for a while now as almost everything gets tagged - you can skip a word. But now it not only carries no signal whatsoever, it turns away people creating original technical content - which is what I assume anti-vibecoding people would actually like to see more of.

Please split it or kill it. But we'd be better off without what exists today.

Added: To be clear, I totally support people filtering out llm-generated or llm-centric posts. But right now everyone loses. And every day we lose a little bit more. Whether it's an original, interesting article that turns out to be nth-degree related to llms and filtered out, or a community member annoyed by this recurring problem and leaving us with even fewer actual non-llm-centric entries.

articles.title: The Brain Sandwich
articles.content: I was on a 1:1 with Emily, one of our strongest engineers, and we were mostly venting about some of the negatives about AI these days: the crazy amount of code reviews, how the job is changing, and the last one (which is the most relevant for this post), how engineers are sometimes completely removing their brains from the equation and just delegating their entire work to AI. (Btw, I heard that the cool kids are calling this a Meat Proxy .) But anyway, the reason I decided to post about this is that Emily has a very simple framework that she uses for working with AI, which she calls the “Brain Sandwich”, that solves this. It’s both about taking full advantage of AI without letting your engineering skills atrophy. The idea is very simple, and can be summarized by: whenever you work on something, you should use: Your brain, and then AI, and then Your brain Explaining a bit more… Before you tell the agent to start building anything, you go there and read and understand it first . You don’t need a complete implementation plan, but you need a rough idea of where you’re going. Otherwise, AI can bias you in the wrong direction. Or even worse, it can nudge you into building something that wasn’t even a problem you needed to solve in the first place! Now that you have all this context, that’s the time to bring AI. By all means, do it. Fully delegate this part with no shame! And when the agent brings you the solution, you will know if it’s right, or if it’s too much, or if it’s completely solving the wrong problem, etc. Then, at the end, your brain comes back. Because before sending your stuff to other people for review, you need to make the work reviewable . Read the diff, check if the complexity is worth it in this case, improve the freaking PR description, etc. The rule of thumb is: if you can’t explain what’s changing and why, it’s not ready for someone else to take a look.

articles.title: ARP! Tell your network to explain itself
articles.content: Hello there! So, I can never remember what IP addresses I have given to devices on my network, or which IP my router has assigned to each one. Recently I’ve been learning about ARP (or Address Resolution Protocol ) and tools like arp-scan, and I wanted to share how cool it is! That’s arp-scan listing every device on my network with its IP, its MAC address, and, most helpful of all, the manufacturer. Here’s how the thing works. So here’s the story. In your local network, when you want to send a message to a device, you need both its IP address and its MAC address. Why would you need two addresses, you ask? That’s a great question, and answering it fully would make this post longer than I want it to be. The briefest answer is that your network switch doesn’t speak IP. All it knows is which devices (identified by their MAC address) are connected to which port. When it receives a packet (technically a frame, but I digress) addressed to some MAC, it forwards it out the physical port that device is plugged into. That's it, that's the bulk of switches' work! Anyway, I bet you’ve never typed ping AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF either. Ain’t nobody got time for that! ping only takes an IP, so how does your computer know the MAC address for 192.168.88.140 when you ping it? Well, it asks, literally! Take a look at this conversation in Wireshark: Even though I only ran a ping command, some communication happens first, and that’s ARP. It all starts with my computer asking everybody on the network, "Hey, who has 192.168.88.140?" That message is broadcast, meaning it’s sent to every device on the network. My network is well behaved, so only the right recipient answered: my Xerox printer, saying, “I have 192.168.88.140, and my MAC address is .....” (My workstation has an AsRock motherboard, if you’re wondering where the source MAC came from.) With that, my computer has everything it needs to send the ping with both the IP and the MAC in the packet. As your computer talks to other devices on the local network, it builds a list of all the neighbors it knows. On Linux you can see that list with ip neighbour show . If you want to watch your computer ask for the MAC of a neighbor it doesn’t know, you can make it forget everything with sudo ip neighbour flush all . This mechanism has some interesting consequences. What if I have an impostor who claims to be 192.168.88.1? Good question. Look up ARP spoofing. 😉 Also, every device receives that broadcast. What if a misbehaving device sends broadcast messages nonstop? Look up broadcast storms, and be responsible with what you learn! 😎 That’s ARP in a nutshell. Next time your network feels like a mystery, just ask it.

articles.title: Outside the Scope of Our Support
articles.content: A few days ago I wrote about reporting a bug to Google Disability Support. It's a bug that kills touch exploration for every screen reader on Android until you reboot the phone. In return I was asked to turn TalkBack off and on again, clear the cache of an app I don't use, and reboot, which is the one thing I'd already told them was the only workaround. If you haven't read that one, Have You Tried Turning TalkBack Off and On Again? has the whole story, and this post won't make much sense without it. There's been more since. I'm going to go through it, because the ending is better than anything I could have made up. But I can tell you how I feel about it in four words, so I'll get them out of the way now. Quite simply, fuck you. Where we left it When I published the first post, I'd answered every question Google's support team asked. I'd done every troubleshooting step they gave me, including the ones that couldn't possibly work, and reported the results. They'd said that once I'd done that, the case could be forwarded to their internal team for further review. So I did it, and I waited to be forwarded. I didn't only wait. The bug happened again the next morning, and this time I was ready for it. I took a full bug report while the phone was stuck. I captured every log buffer, before and after. I worked out exactly why the fake finger gets left on the screen: TouchExplorer gets itself into a dragging state with no valid pointer, tries to build an up event with no pointers in it, MotionEvent throws, the exception gets swallowed, and the up event that would have lifted the finger is never sent. I worked out why nothing short of a reboot clears it: the input dispatcher keeps the record of injected pointers in a verifier that is only ever thrown away when a display is removed, so turning accessibility off, turning every accessibility service off, even tearing down the whole input filter does nothing. I proved that on the phone. I found a way to clear it from the shell with a single cancel event, and a way for a screen reader to clear it with no special permissions at all. And then I wrote fixes, one patch for the accessibility code in frameworks/base and one for the input dispatcher in frameworks/native, and sent a summary of all of it back to the case, along with a request, again, for some way to get the files to an engineer, because their form still wouldn't take anything that wasn't a screenshot. That's a root cause, a recovery method, two patches and a reproduction you can trigger on demand, all done for free, on my own time, on a phone I could only half use. The second agent The next reply came from a different agent, stepping in for the first. And I'll be fair here, because I want to be: it was the best reply I'd had. It read like someone had actually read what I'd sent. articles.title: My obituary for programming
articles.content: My obituary for programming October 8, 2026 Tags: AI , Programming I know, I'm late to this. I was very slow to use AI coding agents. It seems like a lot of programmers never actually liked programming and are thrilled to have a machine do it for them. But I like programming! That's the fun part! Even for programmers who like programming, I know a lot of people feel like they have to use AI to keep up with the competition, especially in a tough job market. But my business is actually having one of its best years ever. So I figured, if I like programming, why not keep programming? I wasn't blind to what was going on around me, though. A lot of slop and hype, but a lot of real stuff too. Engineers I have respected for years saying they no longer write code. Non-programmers accomplishing things that previously would have been far beyond their grasp. And skilled programmers accomplishing truly incredible feats. I couldn't avoid it forever. Eventually I tried it. I can just give it a bug report or an error log entry, and almost instantly it pinpoints the issue and fixes it? I can tell it to try making my code faster, and suddenly it runs 2x or 3x as fast? I can kindly ask it to do that big refactoring I've been putting off for years, and it just does it? But if the AI can refactor my code so easily, did it even matter? I like programming, right? I've been fascinated with computers as long as I can remember. We have these incredible machines that can do absurdly complex calculations for us, but only if we are clever enough to give them the exact right instructions. With a little practice at writing those instructions, I was able to do things that would have been completely infeasible for even the smartest pre-computer genius. It was a real life superpower. articles.title: How Discover-Tech turned targeted ads into a pipeline for zero-click spywares
articles.content: Key Findings Devices at international news network Al Jazeera were infected with mercenary spyware from Candiru (rebranded as “Integrity Labs”) via targeted online advertisements. We provide the first public technical confirmation of a zero-click mercenary spyware attack delivered via targeted advertising, which we call AdFection . The malicious advertisements were purchased by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company that presents itself as a legitimate advertising company, but which we found operates as a facilitator for multiple mercenary spyware partners. Discover-Tech operates a platform called Controlium that enables its mercenary partners to de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices the moment an advertisement is rendered — a form of zero-click attack. Analysis of four billion Discover-Tech bidding records shows that during a four-month period, the company’s ads were shown on almost 200,000 unique websites and Android/iOS apps in dozens of countries. Discover-Tech’s ads also covertly directed millions of devices to contact Candiru’s servers, likely for large-scale tracking and reconnaissance. Discover-Tech is linked to mercenary spyware and intelligence threat actors beyond Candiru, including Intelos and Bindecy. A separate threat actor we call DARK CARTOGRAPHER is using Discover-Tech’s infrastructure to exploit vulnerabilities across numerous mobile carriers to link device advertising IDs with phone numbers, mass-deanonymizing internet users. We will detail our findings concerning this threat actor in a separate forthcoming report. Discover-Tech has appeared on lists of “certified” and “approved” vendors maintained by Google and advertising industry association IAB Europe, and has served ads via major networks such as Google, Yandex, and Beeswax. Discover-Tech has also leveraged the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) consent frameworks to target users within the European Union. Discover-Tech’s mass abuse, privacy invasion, and facilitation for mercenary spyware attacks illustrates structural flaws with the online advertising system, which failed to detect or prevent the abuse documented in this report. We call on regulators to investigate whether Discover-Tech and Candiru/Integrity Labs violated applicable laws, and make recommendations to lawmakers, defenders, and the advertising industry on how to stop AdFection-style attacks and espionage. We disclosed our findings to ad vendors and industry organizations. articles.title: Ghidra + CBMC = Assembly Model Checker
articles.content: ASMC https://github.com/philzook58/asmc is another attempt to glue lifted Ghidra assembly semantics into CBMC. The C Bounded Model Checker https://github.com/diffblue/cbmc is a useful tool on the pareto frontier of soundness, scalability, and pragmatism. I think it’s really cool . CBMC has an intermediate representation call GOTO IR and object file format .gb . asmc-lift takes a compiled .elf file and lifts it into a .gb file using the ghidra pcode semantics as packaged by Trail of Bits https://github.com/lifting-bits/sleigh (Hi Eric!). asmc itself is a driver program that runs asmc-lift and other CBMC tools to actually perform model checking. What I like about this is that it, like CBMC, is flexible for many use cases (standalone assembly verification, translation validation, linking to external assembly, C specs for assembly, DWARF debug data verification, patched assembly verification, decompilation verification) and actually a fairly small amount of glue C++ code for the main lifting tool itself (~1kLOC). GOTO and P-Code are pretty similar. Ultimately many of the questions we want to ask of assembly are about its interaction with C level concepts, or are more simply expressed / specced at something akin to C, so tight integration with CBMC is super useful. Basic Examples Mov 42 Here is a most basic example. We move 42 into rax (the return register) %% file / tmp / mov42 . s . text . globl myfun myfun : mov $ 42 , % rax ret We can run it and check tat 42 is indeed returned. The driver under the hood is calling CC and linking an assembly file. We could also give a preassembled .elf . The post condition string is basically spliced into a CBMC assertion in C, so the assertion language is C. For more complex stuff we want to write a harness ! asmc / tmp / mov42 . s -- function myfun -- post 'outreg.rax == 42' Output: /home/philip/philzook58.github.io/_drafts/asmc-out/myfun-kdgw9qv7 assemble: /home/philip/philzook58.github.io/_drafts/asmc-out/myfun-kdgw9qv7/assemble.log ELF: /home/philip/philzook58.github.io/_drafts/asmc-out/myfun-kdgw9qv7/target.elf Harness: /home/philip/philzook58.github.io/_drafts/asmc-out/myfun-kdgw9qv7/demo.c (x86-64 SysV) Checking: 1 postcondition(s), safety and scalar ABI obligations. seed: /home/philip/philzook58.github.io/_drafts/asmc-out/myfun-kdgw9qv7/seed.log lift: /home/philip/philzook58.github.io/_drafts/asmc-out/myfun-kdgw9qv7/lift.log ASMC lift range: myfun has no ELF size; reachable code window in .text [0x401000, 0x401008) link: /home/philip/philzook58.github.io/_drafts/asmc-out/myfun-kdgw9qv7/link.log cbmc: /home/philip/philzook58.github.io/_drafts/asmc-out/myfun-kdgw9qv7/cbmc.log PASS: all checked properties passed with unwinding assertions This of course should fail. ! asmc / tmp / mov42 . s -- function myfun -- post 'outreg.rax == 43' Output: /home/philip/philzook58.github.io/_drafts/asmc-out/myfun-ej9b_2i2 assemble: /home/philip/philzook58.github.io/_drafts/asmc-out/myfun-ej9b_2i2/assemble.log ELF: /home/phil

articles.title: Bug turns one of the biggest fears about Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses into reality
articles.content: Some Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses were recording people’s conversations without the wearer knowing. The recordings occurred without users saying the prompt phrase (“Hey, Meta”), in a bug that Meta says has been fixed. This week, some users reported online that their Ray-Ban Metas were recording without their consent. A person going by Kindly-Audience-137 on Reddit, for example, said this happened to them across three Meta Ray-Bans and that they had the “Respond without Hey Meta” setting turned off. The person said the Meta AI app “saves audio recordings and text transcripts of these conversations in my conversation history.” “I believe this deserves a serious technical investigation. Customers should not have to wonder whether their private conversations are being captured when they have not intentionally activated their glasses’ AI assistant,” the Reddit user said. Android Authority reported the discussions on Tuesday. Later that day it published a response from Meta that read: “This issue has been resolved. People can manage, review, and delete voice logs of their interactions with Meta AI via settings at any time.” Although Meta’s brief message suggests that the bug is fixed, the broader privacy problem remains. Unanswered questions Meta hasn’t said what caused the Ray-Ban Metas to record people without user consent. Reddit user Kindly-Audience-137 said they “first noticed this behavior after a recent firmware update,” but Meta hasn’t confirmed if a faulty update caused the bug. We also don’t know how many Meta smart glasses were affected. There are a few reports online, but Android Authority said it was unable to replicate the problem before Meta said it fixed it. Ars Technica sent Meta a message asking what it’s doing to prevent future bugs like this from happening again and how many devices were affected. We’ll update this article if we hear back. Even a handful of affected devices is cause for concern, though. Before reports of this bug, privacy advocates had already expressed widespread concerns about Meta’s smart glasses, as well as those from other vendors. Beyond the fear that naturally accompanies the release of new technology that features a microphone and camera, Meta’s glasses pushed the boundaries of privacy further with their more inconspicuous look, prompting concern about how easy it could be for someone to secretly record another person. Meta has previously tried to assuage concerns by pointing to the fact that its glasses light up when recording audio or video. But the bug this week shows that even with this light activated, it’s possible for the smart glasses to record inadvertently. Meta’s brief statement does little to alleviate those worries. Meanwhile, the bug lends some credence to reports and trepidation that Ray-Ban Metas are creating recordings without subjects’ knowledge. articles.title: Google Adopts Pyrefly for Faster, More Accurate Python Type Checking
articles.content: Google has replaced its long-standing Python type checker, Pytype, with Pyrefly, an open-source tool originally developed by Meta. The decision was driven by Pyrefly's advantages, including faster and more accurate type checking, and lower infrastructure costs. By Sergio De Simone

articles.title: AWS Introduces Preview of Well-Architected Agent
articles.content: AWS recently announced the preview of the Well-Architected Agent, a service that analyzes environments against Well-Architected best practices and provides prioritized recommendations across cost, security, performance, and reliability. The AI agent can also suggest remediation steps and review infrastructure-as-code before deployment. By Renato Losio
articles.summary: AWS预览Well-Architected Agent，用AI分析环境并给出成本、安全、性能等优先修复建议。

articles.title: AWS Will Run Its European Sovereign Cloud Without the Global Backbone for Several Hours
articles.content: On October 24, AWS will operate its European Sovereign Cloud without a connection to the AWS Global Network backbone, with a team of EU residents and the region’s own hardware and software. AWS says neither of the two systems being severed is operation-critical, and practitioners are divided over whether the exercise answers the question customers are asking. By Steef-Jan Wiggers

articles.title: Reverse Engineer Anything Project Brings AI Agents to Binary Analysis
articles.content: Reverse Engineer Anything (REA) is an open-source project with over 200K GitHub stars that connects coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex to reverse-engineering tools like Ghidra, Hopper, and IDA. The project lets developers inspect compiled binaries, trace function calls, and investigate how applications implement specific features. By Renato Losio
articles.summary: 开源项目REA将Claude Code等编码智能体接入Ghidra、IDA等逆向工具，可分析二进制文件与函数调用。

articles.title: Amazon Acquires DuckLabs and Integrates DuckDB in Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL
articles.content: Amazon has acquired DuckLabs, the company behind the analytical database DuckDB. Co-founders Hannes Mühleisen and Mark Raasveldt will continue to lead the team under AWS. The acquisition aims to enhance the development and reach of DuckDB while maintaining its open-source status. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL gets its first DuckDB-powered feature following the acquisition. By Gianmarco Nalin
articles.summary: 亚马逊收购DuckDB背后的DuckLabs，创始人留任AWS，DuckDB保持开源并集成进Aurora PostgreSQL。

articles.title: Google EnvHarness Enables Self-Evolving Agents to Learn in Dynamics Environments
articles.content: Google researchers open sourced EnvHarness, a framework that dynamically adapts agent-training environments to an agent's weaknesses without modifying the agent, environment, or evaluation system. According to the researchers, this approach can improve both learning effectiveness and efficiency while helping agents overcome their weaknesses. By Sergio De Simone
articles.summary: Google开源EnvHarness框架，可动态调整智能体训练环境以针对其弱点，提升学习效果与效率。

articles.title: Zod Brings In-Process Schema Compilation and a 9x Cut in Memory Footprint
articles.content: Zod is a TypeScript-focused schema validation library that recently released versions 4.5 and 4.6. Key updates include schema compilation for faster data parsing, significant memory usage reductions, and new validation features. The library supports efficient validation processes and remains popular in the JavaScript ecosystem, achieving millions of downloads weekly. By Daniel Curtis
articles.summary: TypeScript校验库Zod发布4.5和4.6版，引入进程内模式编译，解析更快、内存占用降低9倍。

articles.title: Uber Automates Dependency Analysis Across Its Service Mesh
articles.content: Uber has developed an automated dependency analysis system that uses RPC middleware and production metrics to correlate caller and downstream failures. The approach classifies dependencies as fail-close, fail-open, or unknown and addresses limitations of sampled distributed tracing for rare failures across Uber’s large service mesh. By Leela Kumili
articles.summary: Uber开发自动化依赖分析系统，利用RPC中间件和生产指标关联调用方与下游故障，弥补采样追踪不足。

articles.title: AI in Production: Panellists Highlight Silent Failures, Harness Engineering, and Agent Governance
articles.content: A recent InfoQ webinar examined operational challenges in deploying agentic systems. Key points included issues like semantic and embedding drift, which can lead to significant errors. Experts discussed the need for automated code reviews, continuous evaluation of models, and enhanced privacy measures. The session emphasised a strategic approach to deployment and security management. By Olimpiu Pop
articles.summary: InfoQ网络研讨会探讨智能体系统生产运维难题，包括语义漂移、静默失败、自动代码审查与智能体治理。

articles.title: Grafana Applies SLOs and Error Budgets to AI Agent Behaviour
articles.content: Grafana Labs is proposing a familiar reliability engineering approach for one of the less familiar problems in modern software: how to measure whether an AI agent is actually behaving well. By Craig Risi
articles.summary: Grafana Labs提出用SLO和错误预算衡量AI智能体行为是否可靠，将传统可靠性工程引入AI运维。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #539: AI-made midterm ads top $137 million, and 70% carry no AI label
articles.content: Campaigns and PACs have spent more than $137 million on AI-generated or AI-enhanced midterm ads, and about 70% of them carry no AI label, the New York Times reported. The biggest pro-AI super PAC network paid about $20 million to a Nevada company that exists only as a post office box. A new report found 81 of 134 AI models failed a test built from terrorist-style questions. A video game reverse engineering site is closing because AI made the work too easy. Some companies that rushed into AI are now limiting it, and a JAMA study counted 270 million questions doctors asked one AI tool. In the middle: police in Michigan used an AI-generated photo of a teenager to catch a suspect.
articles.summary: 中期选举中AI生成或增强的广告支出超1.37亿美元，约70%未标注AI，最大亲AI超级PAC资金流向空壳公司。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #537: AI models may soon copy themselves onto smart fridges, Anthropic says
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared most since our last issue on October 8, minus the stories we already sent you in the Daily Espresso. The most shared: Anthropic's warning that small AI models may soon be able to copy themselves onto home devices. Also: a large study of what AI coding agents change at real companies, a fight over how to check AI math proofs, creative workers pushing back on AI, and police buying more AI.
articles.summary: Anthropic警告小型AI模型可能很快能自我复制到智能冰箱等家用设备，引发安全担忧。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #536: Top AI models failed a test of inventing new AI research
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared over the past three days. Most of them look ahead: whether AI can do AI research on its own, who gets a say in governing it, how it is moving into war planning, and how it is moving onto personal computers.
articles.summary: AI Weekly第536期汇总专家分享，聚焦AI能否自主做研究、治理话语权、军事规划应用及进入个人电脑等前沿议题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #535: AI got too expensive, so companies are moving to cheaper models
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past three weeks. Three patterns stand out: companies switching models to control cost, large deployments that are now in daily use, and a growing list of places where AI was restricted or removed.
articles.summary: AI Weekly第535期指出AI成本过高，企业转向更便宜模型，并出现大规模日常部署与AI被限制或移除的增多趋势。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #534: Universities cannot grade their way out of AI
articles.content: This week, campus IT leaders voted AI their top priority for the first time, Cambridge refused Turnitin's new terms over AI training on student work, Dartmouth opened an investigation into its own provost's writing, and Ken Griffin gave Carnegie Mellon $3 billion. Student AI use is no longer a future scenario. The useful question for universities is whether they can teach students to work with AI and still certify what those students can do without it. New evidence from tutoring trials, assessment redesigns, student-support systems and campus data deals points to a practical answer.
articles.summary: AI Weekly第534期报道高校IT负责人首次将AI列为首要任务，剑桥拒Turnitin条款，达特茅斯调查教务长写作，学生用AI成常态。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #533: Meta tested human callers behind its AI phone agent
articles.content: The AI story of September 22–28 was not simply that agents became more capable. It was that their hidden handoffs became visible: a supposedly automated call could reach a contractor, a supposedly private prompt or image could reach a reviewer, a monitor could detect an agent long before a person stopped it, and a local app flaw could inherit every permission a user had granted. The new AI Weekly Who’s Who census points to one practical question: when an agent crosses a boundary, who knows—and who can still intervene?
articles.summary: AI Weekly第533期披露Meta的AI电话代理背后有人工接线员，揭示自动化调用、私密提示和监控中的隐藏人工介入。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #531: AI labs shipped agents before agreeing how to report failures
articles.content: The AI story of September 14–20 was not one spectacular model launch. It was the machinery around agents becoming visible: people reading private chats, models writing instructions into their own memory, plugins updating beneath users, and regulators asking how to stop a system after release. The latest AI Weekly Who’s Who census surfaced 535 expert-shared links. We ranked them by consequence and reader relevance, not by raw share count. Here is what mattered last week—and, more importantly, what could move the story from September 22–28.
articles.summary: AI Weekly第531期指出AI实验室在未就故障报告达成一致前就发布代理，暴露隐私读取、模型自写记忆和插件更新等机制问题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #530: Applied AI This Week
articles.content: Companies are giving AI specific jobs: checking security cameras, helping farmers understand their records, searching satellite images, and preparing sales quotes. This edition explains how those tools work, who can use them, and what companies have reported so far.
articles.summary: AI Weekly第530期介绍企业给AI分配具体任务，如监控摄像头、农业记录、卫星图像搜索和销售报价，并说明其运作与反馈。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #529: OpenAI faces 50-plus lawsuits over alleged ChatGPT harm
articles.content: Thirty new complaints come from survivors of a Canadian school shooting. They accuse OpenAI of failing to warn police; the company disputes key claims.
articles.summary: OpenAI因ChatGPT涉嫌伤害面临50多起诉讼，其中30起来自加拿大校园枪击案幸存者，指控其未警告警方，公司否认关键指控。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #528: What are companies building with AI? An Applied AI Deep Dive
articles.content: We went looking for what companies are actually building with AI. The answer was not more chatbots. It was drones carrying diagnostic samples, driverless Frito-Lay trucks, AI-guided flight paths, repair copilots, and rugged GPU laptops in Ukraine. We reviewed 136 use cases from the last 20 days. The biggest surprise: only 38 included a reported outcome.
articles.summary: AI Weekly第528期深挖企业实际AI应用，发现并非聊天机器人，而是诊断无人机、无人卡车、飞行路径和维修副驾等136个用例。

articles.title: From zero to NanoClaw
articles.content: Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project's community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private. They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw's "skills over features" approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam's case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.
articles.summary: NanoClaw创作者Gavriel Cohen讲述40小时周末项目如何成为爆款开源项目，并发展为专注容器隔离安全的企业AI公司。

articles.title: Forking Cal.com to closed source
articles.content: This week I'm joined by Peer Richelsen, co-founder of Cal.com. What if the majority of open source repositories are already compromised and we just don't know it yet? That's the theory Peer brings to the table this week. We dig into how AI has flattened the knowledge graph to the point that a 16-year-old can vibe hack a power station just as easily as their mom can vibe code an iOS app, why the reporting culture that has kept open source safe all these years is collapsing under AI generated noise, Cal.com's move to fork its own codebase and take the sensitive parts private, and the eye opening reality that shipping "$1 of AI tokens for pennies on the dollar" is now a common startup business model.
articles.summary: Cal.com 联合创始人 Peer Richelsen 在播客中提出开源仓库可能已被普遍攻陷的观点，并讨论 AI 对知识获取门槛的冲击。

articles.title: Postgres at PlanetScale
articles.content: Sam Lambert is back after 4 years and he does not hold back! We cover $5 PlanetScale Postgres, the Neki "do-over" of Vitess, agents shipping schema changes through deploy requests, rolling back a 500TB table in seconds, and the very real question of whether to open source any of it. Plus: why he thinks the sleeping, lazy giants should be broken up.
articles.summary: PlanetScale 推出5美元 Postgres 服务，CEO Sam Lambert 介绍 Vitess 重做、AI 代理提交 schema 变更及秒级回滚500TB表。

articles.title: Canary tokens and digital tripwires
articles.content: Haroon Meer is back! Haroon is the Founder of Thinkst, the ~50-person bootstrapped company behind Canary and Canarytokens — honeypots and tripwires you sprinkle inside your network and forget about until an attacker touches one. We talk about the AWS API key token attackers just can't resist trying, the real credit card token backed by an actual bank partnership, Breadcrumbs (their brand-new feature that leads intruders straight to your canaries), a live demo where a hardware Canary becomes a Synology NAS in one click, and how a company with zero outbound sales and no price increase in ten years quietly passed $22.5 million in ARR.
articles.summary: Thinkst 创始人 Haroon Meer 介绍 Canary 蜜罐与数字绊线产品，分享攻击者难以抗拒的 AWS API 密钥诱饵等实战经验。

articles.title: From open source hits to OpenAI
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Max Stoiber, currently working on ChatGPT's plugin directory and app platform at OpenAI. We discuss the hundreds of open source projects nobody remembers alongside the big ones like react-boilerplate and styled-components, how Spectrum became part of GitHub and eventually helped shape GitHub Discussions, the founder growth that came from building Stellate, the GraphQL cache that turned into a dual acquisition by Shopify and The Guild, and why ChatGPT apps feel like a new surface for software.
articles.summary: OpenAI 的 Max Stoiber 回顾 react-boilerplate、styled-components 等开源项目历程，并介绍 ChatGPT 插件目录与平台建设。

articles.title: MCP on Code Mode
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Matt Carey about Code Mode and how most of us have been thinking about MCP all wrong. Matt works on the Agents SDK and MCP at Cloudflare — we discuss how server-side Code Mode lets one MCP server expose all ~2,500 Cloudflare API endpoints in about 1,000 tokens of context, the dynamic Worker loader that runs model-written code safely in a V8 isolate, Matt's own workflow with Claude, where memory fits into the future of agents, and his Zaggy git wrapper that keeps agents from force-pushing his repos.
articles.summary: Cloudflare 的 Matt Carey 介绍 Code Mode，称单个 MCP 服务器可用约1000个 token 暴露全部约2500个 Cloudflare API 端点。

articles.title: Automation at the speed of Swamp
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Adam Jacob, founder of System Initiative and creator of Swamp, about what happens when AI agents change the entire shape of software development. We discuss how he went from an 18-person team down to five and shipped Swamp 900 times in four weeks, why he brought User Acceptance Testing (UAT) testing back from the 90s, why software architecture (and domain-driven design) suddenly matters more than knowing how to write code, the live demo where I pointed Swamp at my Proxmox box and watched it write its own automation (blew my mind!!), and why he'll never accept a pull request to Swamp, ever.
articles.summary: System Initiative 创始人 Adam Jacob 讲述借助 AI 代理将团队从18人缩至5人，并在四周内发布 Swamp 900次。

articles.title: Bitwarden CLI compromised
articles.content: Bitwarden's CLI got hit by the Checkmarx supply-chain campaign, TypeScript 7.0 beta lands with the Go-rewritten compiler running ~10x faster than 6.0, and pgBackRest lost its maintainer of thirteen years leaving anyone running production Postgres with a real dependency-trust task this week. We've also got Ubuntu 26.04 LTS shipping with TPM-backed full-disk encryption, and Matz dropping Spinel as an AOT path that takes Ruby to native binaries. This week was a good reminder that the tools we depend on are all moving at once. Security, performance, and maintenance aren't isolated threads.
articles.summary: Bitwarden CLI 遭 Checkmarx 供应链攻击，TypeScript 7.0 beta 编译器提速约10倍，pgBackRest 维护者离职引发依赖信任问题。

articles.title: Exploring with agents
articles.content: Today on the show I’m talking with Amelia Wattenberger — designer, data-viz veteran, ex-GitHub Next, and now designing Intent at Augment Code. What if the last 30% of any software project is about to become the hardest part you’ve ever done? That’s the argument Amelia is making today. We discuss the identity crisis developers are having as agents take over the keyboard, the epic redesign of developer tooling in this agent-first world, the arc from autocomplete to chat to CLI back to UI, why Intent treats a workspace as their core primitive not a chat thread, the tradeoffs between one-worktree-per-agent vs. one-worktree-per-task, and why she thinks prototyping just got easier but finishing got harder.
articles.summary: 设计师 Amelia Wattenberger 认为 AI 代理将让软件项目最后30%的工作成为最难部分，并分享在 Augment Code 的设计实践。

articles.title: 'Human Vs. Robot' Cage Match Was Illegal, Says California
articles.content: "A human defeated two of the three robots he faced in a cage fight recently held in San Francisco," reports the Los Angeles Times, noting that videos of the event drew more than 10 million views on YouTube. But "the humans behind that fight could face a battle of their own — the legal type — if they want to hold another event like 'Human Vs. Robot,' the Sept. 18 competition that placed influencer Frankie LaPenna inside an octagon to battle three humanoid robots that were controlled remotely by a human operator in separate MMA-style fights..." Wearing spiked gloves, a helmet and protective padding, the 5-foot-6, 205-pound LaPenna held his own against all three bots. He dominated his first opponent, referred to at the fight as "the child robot." Next came an imposing "Terminator"-inspired humanoid, which was listed on the fight video as 6-feet and 200 pounds with a kick force of 850 pounds. The robot landed several hard kicks, including one that knocked LaPenna across the mat and another with an impact that brought the humanoid to the ground and caused its head to come off — but the human seemed to gain strength as the match went on and eventually stood triumphantly with his foot on the machine's crumpled body. LaPenna was dominant early in his final match, in which he faced a robot that resembled a "Predator" from the movies of the same name. After landing several punches and kicks and taking his opponent to the ground multiple times, LaPenna eventually became fatigued and called for the match to be ended. "He doesn't get tired. He doesn't stay down," LaPenna said in a postmatch interview. "The crowd of about 100 (humans, not humanoids) was thrilled," writes the New York Times. (After beating his first robot opponent, LaPenna told his interviewer, "Clankers zero, humans one.") articles.title: Programming Language Popularity Increases for R, Julia, and Rust (but Not Go)
articles.content: TechRepublic reports: The TIOBE Index is a monthly indicator of programming-language popularity based on factors including skilled engineers, courses, and third-party vendors. The October 2026 rankings show a largely stable top 10, with R overtaking SQL and Julia returning to the top 20 for the first time in three years. [SQL has risen to #9 from #10 in October of 2025 — back when R ranked only #13.] Python remains No. 1, followed by C, C++, Java, C#, and JavaScript, while Rust holds its No. 10 position. [A year ago Rust ranked only #16.] Outside the top 10, Julia climbs from No. 21 to No. 18, and TIOBE introduces Mandarin Chinese search terms into its methodology to broaden the index's geographic representation. Dropping out of the top ten is Go, which fell from #8 in October of 2025 to #11. And Delphi/Object Pascal has plummeted from #9 to #19. TIOBE CEO Paul Jansen argues that Julia's growing popularity "is largely driven by the demand for modern programming languages that combine high performance with ease of learning, particularly for numerical computing." Python offers an accessible, high-level approach to numerical computing, but performance can become a bottleneck. C++, on the other hand, delivers excellent performance but comes with a steeper learning curve and a lower level of abstraction. Julia aims to bridge this gap by combining the best of both worlds... Apart from Julia, two other languages are knocking on the door of the TIOBE top 20: Dart and OCaml. Dart jumps from #41 to #27 this month. Thanks to its popular UI toolkit Flutter, Dart has been hovering around the edge of the top 20 for quite some time. OCaml, on the other hand, might come as a surprise. It jumps from #38 to #26 this month, driven in part by its growing use in real-time trading systems and parsing technology. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: FSF Criticizes Raspberry Pi DRM Blocking RAM Upgrades
articles.content: The Free Software Foundation "has never supported Raspberry Pi," writes their deputy directory Sean O'Brien, "as it depends on nonfree software for the boot process, leaving an important part of the computer outside the user's control." But they're now decrying "an even more intrusive restriction on user freedom" — the binary-blob bootloader changes that limit your ability to upgrade RAM: The restriction is not new: the relevant checks were introduced in the device firmware around 2024. However, these hardware handcuffs have only recently received wider attention. Unscrupulous sellers have reportedly replaced memory on lower-capacity boards and resold them as more expensive models, sometimes using unreliable or defective components. articles.title: Mutative v2  - better immutability and faster immutable updates
articles.content: Mutative 2.0 is out. Read the release notes , the announcement and the migration guide from v1 to v2 . Mutative - A JavaScript library for efficient immutable updates ( documentation ). In the benchmark , it was about 3.6x faster than Immer with the same settings and 6.6x faster with each library's defaults across 97 workloads. In that benchmark the gap widened on large arrays, where Mutative moved elements up to 1,052x faster than Immer. When copying dominates, such as updating objects with thousands of keys, inserting at the front of a large array or adding an item to a large Set, Mutative is even faster than hand-written reducers. How does Mutative compare with the spread operation (hand-written reducers)? Mutative copies each object at most once per update, however many changes a recipe makes. Immer made it easy to write immutable updates as mutations of a draft. Mutative keeps that model and focuses on performance: it copies each object at most once per update, drafts objects only when a recipe reads them, finalizes only the drafts that changed, and runs array methods that move elements natively on its copies. Immer freezes the next state by default, which costs time on every update; Mutative freezes it only when asked to. Mutative also takes its options per call instead of from global configuration, drafts class instances through marks instead of changing their classes, supports async recipes and Map and Set subclasses, and handles edge cases that Immer gets wrong. Comparison with Immer lists the differences. Mutative passed all of Immer's test cases. Mutative 2.0.0 was 3.6x faster than Immer 11.1.18 with matched settings and 6.6x faster with each library's defaults, on geometric mean across 97 benchmarked workloads, and faster in 595 of 614 measured cases. The gap grows on large arrays, where Mutative moves elements natively: removing the first of 10,000 rows took 7.04 µs, against 7,408 µs. The performance summary has the complete results, the method, and their limits. Selected results The benchmark suite times 99 workloads: Immer's own performance tests, array methods, reads, Map and Set values, object records, class instances, a deep path, patch application, returned values, and searches. Its last full run measured 97 of them, and a focused run the two that return fresh data. It compares Mutative with Immer 11.1.18 and with reducers written by hand, after checking every result against those reducers. With matched settings, both libraries freeze or both do not, and both generate patches or both do not. With each library's defaults, Mutative without auto-freeze and Immer with it, Mutative was faster in 154 of 157 cases. The other 3 return a state that Immer froze earlier: Immer skips frozen values when it searches a returned state for drafts, while Mutative, which does not freeze by default, searches it unless the recipe wraps it in rawReturn() , which took 0.26 µs. Times are microseconds per update, medians of three runs on an Apple M1 Ma

articles.title: theAuth: open-source TypeScript auth for AI agents, with an MCP OAuth 2.1 server
articles.content: Open-source auth where AI agents are first class. Agent identity, delegation with live revocation and an MCP OAuth 2.1 server, next to the usual human sign in. One TypeScript library, self-hosted, MIT licensed. Website · Quickstart · Docs · Examples · Discussions · GLINR Discord theAuth is auth for products where AI agents act on behalf of people. Each agent gets its own identity and a bearer token, scoped permissions, an owner, and an audit row for every decision. An agent can hand a subset of its permissions to another agent, and revoking any link in that chain takes effect on the next call. It includes an OAuth 2.1 authorization server for MCP, and the usual human sign in: email and password, magic links, passkeys, TOTP, 48 OAuth providers, SAML and OIDC SSO, SCIM. It runs on Node, Bun, Deno and Cloudflare Workers with four runtime dependencies ( drizzle-orm , jose , sql.js , zod ). No hosted service is required. articles.title: Type-safe OpenAPI requests that follow your document exactly
articles.content: openapi-chain compiles the serialization rules an OpenAPI document declares (parameter style , explode , allowReserved and content , request media types, and form and multipart Encoding Objects) and applies them to every request. A build-time CLI generates types and metadata scoped to the paths you call, so large documents stay affordable to type-check and to ship. Calls use a fluent path API with no generated endpoint code and no runtime dependencies. The pnpm monorepo contains three publishable packages: openapi-chain , @openapi-chain/cli , and @openapi-chain/query . The runtime keeps its existing package name and entry points. See the package migration guide for CLI and query import changes and release availability. The first request below uses the Items schema . Your chain follows your own schema: static path segments become properties, {parameters} become function calls, and HTTP methods become request functions. Exact wire serialization: the strict client sends what the document specifies and rejects representations it cannot encode instead of guessing. The wire comparison executes 20 declarations through both clients: openapi-fetch 0.17.0 sends a request with different values, media type or missing parameters in 16 of them, and differs only in percent-encoding or list spacing in 3 more. Scoped generation for large documents: one CLI config produces full declarations, a path scope and matching runtime metadata. On the pinned GitHub REST document, scoping a 40-operation consumer reduced openapi-chain's TypeScript 7 check time from 0.49 s to 0.045 s ( real-schema measurements ). Typed requests and responses: infer parameters, request media types and status-correlated results from the selected operation. Keep openapi-fetch if you already use it: openapi-chain/openapi-fetch applies the same serialization to an existing openapi-fetch client ( adapter guide ). Small schema-free core: the default client has a 3.5 KiB gzip budget , enforced by a reproducible size check ; its bundle size and per-request overhead are in the same range as openapi-fetch ( client comparison ). Customizable requests: operation-typed extensions and Fetch-compatible transports support application-specific serialization, authentication and parsing. When to choose openapi-chain Choose the strict client when your document declares non-default parameter styles, parameter content , cookie parameters, non-JSON media types or form and multipart encoding, and the server depends on them. Choose the CLI's scoped generation when a large document makes type-checking or metadata delivery expensive. If your API only uses JSON bodies and default parameter styles, openapi-fetch and openapi-chain's core are comparable in size and speed; pick the call style you prefer. Without scoping, openapi-chain's fluent types cost more to check than openapi-fetch's on the measured GitHub and Stripe documents. For a published release with this API: pnpm add openapi-chain pnpm add -D @openapi-chain/cli S

articles.content: Home / Node.js Node.js built-ins that replaced npm packages By Flavio Copes Sep 20, 2026 Twelve Node.js built-ins that replace axios, nodemon, dotenv, jest, chalk, glob and more, with their stability in Node 24 and one gotcha each. ~~~ Open a package.json from a few years ago and you’ll find the same names in almost every one. axios , nodemon , dotenv , jest , chalk , uuid , rimraf . Node.js now ships a built-in for each of them. Here are twelve of those built-ins, with the package each one replaces, the shortest example that runs, how stable it is in the current LTS line, and the one thing the old package still does that the built-in doesn’t. Several of these changed status in the last year, so I checked every claim against the Node 24 API docs (24.21.0, the Active LTS line as of September 2026) and ran every example on Node 26.0.0, which is what node --version prints on my Mac. Node 22 is in maintenance until April 2027, Node 20 reached end of life on April 30, 2026, and Node 26 becomes the next LTS on October 28, 2026. Where Node 22 and 24 differ, I say so. A quick reminder on how Node labels its APIs. Stability 2 is stable. Stability 1 is experimental, with sub-levels: 1.0 is early development, 1.1 is active development, 1.2 is a release candidate. Anything experimental can change or disappear in a minor release, so the number matters if you’re putting it in production. 1. node:sqlite replaces better-sqlite3 For years the way to use SQLite from Node was better-sqlite3 , a native addon you had to compile (or download a prebuilt binary for) on every install. Node 22.5 added a SQLite driver to core. Like better-sqlite3 , it’s synchronous, so the code reads top to bottom with no await . import { DatabaseSync } from 'node:sqlite' const db = new DatabaseSync ( '/Users/flavio/notes.db' ) db. exec ( 'CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS notes (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, body TEXT)' ) const insert = db. prepare ( 'INSERT INTO notes (body) VALUES (?)' ) insert. run ( 'Buy espresso beans' ) console. log (db. prepare ( 'SELECT * FROM notes' ). all ()) The module only exists under the node: prefix, a plain import 'sqlite' fails. Status in Node 24: 1.2, release candidate , since 24.15.0. It prints no warning. In Node 22 it’s still 1.1, active development (the --experimental-sqlite flag went away in 22.13, the label didn’t), so a server on Node 22 is running an API the docs describe as “nearing minimum viability”. Where it does less: better-sqlite3 has db.transaction(fn) , which wraps a function in BEGIN , COMMIT and ROLLBACK for you, and node:sqlite has nothing like it. You write those three statements yourself in a try / catch . I show the pattern in node:sqlite: SQLite built into Node.js , and the free SQLite course covers transactions and indexes in more depth. 2. node:test and node:assert replace Jest and Mocha Jest was the default test runner for a long time, and I have a whole post on it from 2018. articles.title: Tibetan-Singing-Bowls: Strike or rub a set of virtual Tibetan singing bowls - synthesized in the browser with Web Audio, with the beating overtones of the real thing
articles.content: Play a set of virtual Tibetan singing bowls right in your browser. Strike a bowl, or hold it down to draw the tone out the way a mallet circles the rim. The sound is synthesized live, so there are no audio files to load, and it works offline. Use headphones or good speakers. Seven bowls are tuned to a scale, each with its own color. Tap or click a bowl to strike it. Switch to Sing and hold a bowl down to make it swell and sustain, then let go to let it fade. The number keys 1 to 7 play the bowls from the keyboard, and you can play several at once. Tuning : a seven-note chakra scale (C to B, one bowl per chakra) or a pentatonic scale, in the low, middle or high octave, with A at 440 Hz or 432 Hz. Sound : volume and room reverb. Spectrum : a live view of the sound, so you can watch the overtones rise and fade. Sound bath : press start and pick 5, 10, 20 or 30 minutes, and the bowls play by themselves, one strike at a time, with silence in between. A struck bowl rings at its fundamental plus overtones at about 2.7, 5.2 and 8.3 times that pitch. Those overtones are not whole-number multiples, which is why a bowl sounds like a bell and not like a string. Each partial is made of two sine oscillators a fraction of a hertz apart, so it swells and fades a few times a second: that beating is the "wah-wah" of a real bowl. Higher partials die away faster. The result goes through a synthesized room reverb and a compressor. This is a model of the sound and not a recording. The bowls are not meant as a medical treatment, and the chakra colors are a common convention, not a measurement. The pages are plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with the Web Audio API, with no dependencies and no build step. Just open index.html . It is also a small installable web app: add it to your home screen or desktop and it works offline. The bowls are drawn as SVG. The app logic is in js/bowls.js . Three color themes (dark, light and blue) are shared with my other projects. Your tuning, volume and other settings are kept in the browser's local storage. articles.title: Supapower - A sync engine that keeps a local PGlite database in sync with Supabase, inspired by PowerSync
articles.content: Supapower is a sync engine that keeps a local PGlite database in sync with Supabase , so an application can read and write locally and stay usable while offline. It is inspired by PowerSync . Status: 0.3.0. Both directions of the sync work; the public API may still change before 1.0. Nothing new to deploy - Supabase's Data API and Realtime are the sync protocol; no sync service, no replication slot, no second bill. Real Postgres on both ends - the client is PGlite, not SQLite: the same SQL, the same types, and migrations you can lift from the server. Your RLS policies are the sync rules - downloads and writes go through PostgREST as the signed-in user, so there is no second authorization language to keep in step. Two-way sync that merges per column - offline writes queue per transaction and upload only the columns that changed, so two people editing different fields of a row both keep their edit. Three lines to adopt - a PGlite extension plus one sync() call; no codegen, no schema DSL, no client-side query language to learn. Small, permissive, batteries included - Apache-2.0 with zero runtime dependencies, plus a SharedWorker multi-tab host, React and Vue bindings, and a typed status and event API. Longer version, and how it compares with RxDB, PowerSync, Electric and Zero: supapower.dev/why-supapower · supapower.dev/comparison Everything below, except the examples section , is for working with the monorepo. For documentation on the Supapower library see the supapower package's readme , or the full documentation site at supapower.dev . Package Description supapower The main package for Supapower - a PGlite extension that integrates with Supabase and syncs data between them @supapower/worker A more stable drop-in replacement for PGlite's built-in multi-tab worker, using a SharedWorker with automatic fallback - works with plain PGlite, no Supapower required @supapower/react React hooks for Supapower: PGlite live queries plus sync status @supapower/vue Vue composables for Supapower: PGlite live queries plus sync status Example Description chat A terminal chat app, showing a two-way sync between Supabase and PGlite vue-chat A browser chat app, showing @supapower/worker 's multi-tab SharedWorker and a two-way sync between Supabase and PGlite Bun 1.4 or later, used as package manager, test runner and script runner Node.js 22 or later or a modern browser for consumers of the published packages bun install bun run check bun run check runs the same four steps as continuous integration: lint, format check, typecheck and tests. Script What it does bun run build Compiles every package to dist with the TypeScript compiler bun run typecheck Typechecks every package, tests included bun test Runs the test suite with the Bun test runner bun run test:coverage Runs the test suite and reports coverage bun run lint Lints with Oxlint bun run lint:fix Lints and applies the fixes Oxlint can make safely bun run format Formats the repository with Oxfmt bun run format:chec

articles.title: 今天开车被迫窝囊了一次
articles.content:
开车等红灯，还剩三四十秒时，前车往前跑了一段，空了大概十几米距离。我没动，准备快变灯时再起步过去。



这时候后面车开始滴滴滴打喇叭，我想着反正红灯又走不了，就没理他。随后他一个猛拐，从左车道饶过我去前面了，我还是没在意，又走不了，你想塞就塞呗。



此时我前面有两辆车。绿灯亮了，大家正常起步，我跟在后面。这时有意思的事情发生了：前车压上斑马线后，突然一个急刹不动了，过了四五秒，又挪了一下，随后又是一脚刹停。



我一下子明白了，感情这是报复我来了。就这样，他一直卡到黄灯才走。我这时还比较淡定，只是随口骂了句 SB ，心想：这不是给我送证据让我举报吗？装了这么久的海康威视行车记录仪终于要派上用场了。我还特意瞄了眼时间，方便后面找视频。



下车时，我把内存卡拔了下来，带回家，翻出尘封已久的读卡器，连上电脑。然后就傻眼了：这特么什么情况？怎么那个时间段一个视频都没有？要说坏了，但是后面还有新的视频，卡也没满啊？



不死心，又翻了几遍其它目录，最后确定没有。不过倒是发现了一个规律：这记录仪好像每次只会记录起步和停车的几分钟，中间全是空的？不是哥们，这科学吗？



这下子尴尬了，本以为能重拳出击呢，没想到小丑竟是我自己，只能窝囊忍着了。



给 V 友们丢脸了 😭

articles.title: AI 发现了我的睡不好的原因
articles.content:
从今年 6 月开始，我一直睡眠不好：晚上睡不安稳、频繁醒来，而且每次醒来都觉得口干舌燥。

一开始以为是夏天天热，没太在意。但现在天气凉了，症状还是这样。我就去了几趟医院：

挂了内分泌科和肾内科做检查，各项指标都没查出异常。
网上查到可以去睡眠科做监测，一问价格一晚要三五千，直接被劝退。

几趟医院折腾下来，不仅睡眠越来越差，心里也开始焦虑，总怀疑自己是不是得了什么查不出来的怪病。

后来我把时间线梳理了一下：症状正好是从 6 月份开始打替尔泊肽之后出现的。虽然之前复诊时顺嘴问过医生，医生当时明确表示跟打针没关系，但我还是决定核实一下。

我从网上搜到了替尔泊肽的完整药品说明书，扔给 AI ，并说了我最近的症状。发现了替尔泊肽的这些副作用：

1. 夜间低血糖：部分人在使用替尔泊肽后可能出现夜间低血糖，进而引发多梦、易醒；
2. 脱水与口干：少数人群在用药期间会出现明显的口干反应。

这两点跟我的症状一模一样。

虽然医生也是专业的，但可能更关注常见的检查出来的指标数据，对少数不良反应不会第一时间到。反而是让 AI 结合完整说明书，找到了盲区。

知道原因后，心里瞬间不焦虑了。记录一下这次经历，算是 AI 在日常健康的一个例子。
